en: Mahāniddesa,
Aṭṭhakavagga, 11.
Explanation of the Discourse on Quarrels and Disputes (Kalahavivādasuttaniddesa)
Now he will explain the exposition of the *Kalahavivāda-sutta*:
From what do quarrels and disputes arise,
along with lamentations, sorrows, and envy?
Pride, arrogance, and slander—whence have these arisen for you? Tell me this at once.
Whence have quarrels and disputes arisen?
There is quarreling in one way; dispute is also just that.
That which is quarreling is dispute; that which is dispute is quarreling.
Alternatively, in another sense, "dispute" (vivāda) is said to be the preliminary stage of quarreling (kalaha).
Kings dispute with kings, kshatriyas dispute with kshatriyas, brahmins dispute with brahmins, householders dispute with householders;
even a mother disputes with her son, and a son disputes with his mother.
They dispute: the father disputes with the son, the son disputes with the father;
the brother disputes with the brother, the brother disputes with the sister, the sister disputes with the brother; the companion disputes with the companion—this is dispute.
What is quarreling?

Householders, seeking to strike with sticks, engage in quarreling by means of body or speech; those who have gone forth, having committed an offense, engage in quarreling by means of body or speech—this is quarreling.
"From where are quarrels and disputes brought forth?
From where are quarrels and disputes brought forth, from where born, from where arisen, from where produced, from where fully manifested, from where made manifest?
What is their source, what is their origin, what is their birth, what is their provenance?"—thus regarding quarrels and disputes.
And he asks about the root, asks about the cause, asks about the source, asks about the origin, asks about the provenance,
asks about the origination, asks about the nutriment, asks about the object,
asks about the condition, asks about the arising; he inquires, questions, requests, entreats, and persuades.
From where have quarrels and disputes arisen?
And lamentation and sorrow, together with envy?
"Lamentation" refers to that which occurs when one is afflicted by the loss of relatives, the loss of wealth, or the loss of health.
Whether one is touched by misfortune through loss of relatives, or touched by misfortune through loss of wealth, or touched by misfortune through impairment of morality,
or touched by misfortune through impairment of view, or possessed of some other kind of misfortune, or touched by some other painful condition— there is weeping, lamentation,
the act of weeping, the act of lamentation, the state of having wept, the state of having lamented, and the babbling, the prattling, the wailing of speech.
Lamentation is the state of lamenting.
Sorrow is the sorrow of one who is afflicted by the loss of relatives, or afflicted by the loss of wealth, health, virtue, or view;
or of one who possesses some other misfortune, or is touched by some other painful condition.
Sorrowing, the state of having sorrowed, inward sorrow, inward anguish, inward burning, inward fever, the consuming of the mind,
mental distress, and the dart of sorrow.
Avarice refers to the five kinds of avarice:
Stinginess regarding dwellings, stinginess regarding families, stinginess regarding gains, stinginess regarding praise, and stinginess regarding the Dhamma. Whatever such stinginess,
being stingy, state of being stingy, concealment, meanness, harshness, and the state of being ungrasping in the mind—
this is called stinginess.
Moreover, stinginess regarding the aggregates is stinginess; stinginess regarding the elements is stinginess; stinginess regarding the sense bases is stinginess, which is grasping.
This is called stinginess—lamentation and sorrow together with stinginess.
"Conceit, overweening conceit, and slander. Here,
"conceit" (māna) refers to when someone generates pride on account of birth, or clan, or family lineage,
or physical beauty, or wealth, or Vedic study, or field of occupation, or craft, or branch of science, or learning.
Or by wit, or by some other basis. *Atimāna* (conceit):
here someone holds another in contempt on account of birth, or clan, or... [as before] ...or by some other basis.
*Pesuñña* (slander): here someone is a speaker of divisive speech—
Having heard something here, one reports it there for the purpose of dividing these people; or having heard something there, one reports it here for the purpose of dividing those people.

Thus, being a divider of those who are united, or an instigator of those who are divided, delighting in factions, rejoicing in factions, finding pleasure in factions, one utters speech that creates factions—this is called malicious talebearing.
Moreover, one instigates malicious talebearing for two reasons:
either out of a desire for favor or with the intention of causing a rift.
How does one instigate malicious talebearing out of a desire for favor?
Thinking, "I will become dear to him, I will become pleasing to him, I will become trustworthy, I will become intimate, I will become well-disposed toward him"—
thus one engages in slander out of a desire for affection.
How does one engage in slander with the intention of causing division?
"How might these [people] become divided, separated, factionalized, split, alienated, and fall into two parties;

how might they break apart and not come together, and live in suffering rather than in comfort?"—it is with such an intention toward division that one engages in slander. Thus: "Pride and arrogance, along with slander."
“From where have these been summoned? Pray, tell me that.
“Quarrel, dispute, lamentation, sorrow, stinginess, conceit, arrogance, and slander—wherefrom have these eight defilements been summoned? From where are they born? From where do they arise?
From where are they produced? From where are they generated? From where do they become manifest? What is their source? What is their origin? What is their birth? What is their provenance?”
He asks about the root of these eight defilements; he asks about their cause, their source, their origin,
their provenance, their origination, their nutriment, their object, their condition, their arising— he inquires, questions, requests, entreats, and seeks to clarify them.
"From where have they come to you? Tell me that, please!
Tell it, explain it, point it out, establish it, reveal it, analyze it, make it clear, and manifest it—tell me that, please:
from where have they come to you?"
Therefore that created being said:
“From what have quarrels and disputes arisen,
along with lamentations, sorrows, and envy?
“From where have pride, arrogance, and slander arisen for you? Pray, tell me that.
“Quarrels and disputes arise from abundance of what is dear.”
Lamentations and sorrows together with envy;
conceit and arrogance along with slander;
quarrels and disputes joined with stinginess.
And there are slanders arising from disputes.
Quarrels and disputes abound because of what is dear; likewise lamentation, sorrow, and envy. "What is dear" refers to two kinds of the dear: [the dear person and the dear object].
Either beings or formations.
Which beings are dear?

Here, those who wish for one’s welfare, wish for one’s benefit, wish for one’s comfort, and wish for one’s security from bondage—whether they be mother, father, brother, sister, son, daughter, friend, minister, relative, or kinsman.
These beings are dear.
Which formations are dear?
Agreeable forms, agreeable sounds, agreeable odors, agreeable tastes, and agreeable tangibles.
These formations are dear.
Even those fearing the loss of a dear object engage in quarreling; they engage in quarreling when it is being lost, and they engage in quarreling when it has been lost.
Even those fearing the change of a dear object engage in quarreling; they engage in quarreling when it is changing, and they engage in quarreling when it has changed.
They quarrel over a beloved object when they fear its loss, they quarrel while it is being lost, and they quarrel once it has been lost.
They quarrel over a beloved object when they fear its change, they quarrel while it is changing, and they quarrel once it has changed.
They lament over a beloved object when they fear its loss, they lament while it is being lost, and they lament once it has been lost.
They lament over a beloved object when they fear its change, they lament while it is changing, and they lament once it has changed.
They grieve over a beloved object when they fear its loss, they grieve while it is being lost, and they grieve once it has been lost.
They grieve over a beloved object when they fear its change, they grieve while it is changing, and they grieve once it has changed.
They guard, protect, grasp, treat as "mine," and are possessive toward a dear object.
And there are conceit and overweening conceit together with slander.
Relying on a dear object, they generate conceit; relying on a dear object, they generate overweening conceit.
How do they generate conceit based on a pleasing object?
They think, "We are possessors of desirable forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
In this way, they generate conceit based on a pleasing object.
How do they generate excessive conceit based on a pleasing object?
They think: "We are obtainers of pleasant forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, whereas these others are not obtainers of pleasant forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
In this way, they generate excessive conceit based on a pleasing object.
Slander (*pesuñña*) means: here someone is a slanderer; having heard something from one person, he reports it to another for the purpose of dividing them...
[as before] ...thus, with the intention of causing division, he engages in slander...
[as before] ...along with pride and arrogance, and accompanied by slander.
"Those associated with stinginess are quarrels and disputes.
Quarrel, dispute, lamentation, sorrow, conceit, overweening pride, and slander—
these seven defilements are joined, bound, yoked, and fully engaged with stinginess.
"Strife and disputes are joined with stinginess.
And among those born of dispute are backbitings.
When a dispute has arisen, been produced, come into being, fully manifested, and become apparent, they bring forth backbiting.
Having heard here, they report it there for the sake of dividing these people; or having heard there, they report it here for the sake of dividing those people.

Thus, they are dividers of those who are united, or instigators of those who are already divided; delighting in factions, rejoicing in factions, finding pleasure in factions, they utter speech that creates factions—this is called malicious talebearing (*pesuñña*).
Moreover, they engage in slander for two reasons:
either out of a desire for affection or with the intention of causing division.
How do they engage in slander out of a desire for affection?
"We shall become dear to him, we shall become pleasing to him, we shall become trusted by him, we shall become insiders, we shall become well-disposed toward him.
It is with such a desire for affection that they engage in slander.
How do they engage in slander with the intention of causing division?

“How might these [people] become divided, separated, factional, split, alienated, and fall into two parties; how might they break apart and not come together, and dwell in suffering rather than in comfort?”— thus,
by instigating malicious talebearing with the intent to cause division among those engaged in disputes, one engages in malicious talebearing.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“From abundance of what is dear arise quarrels and disputes,
lamentations and sorrows, along with avarice.”
Pride and arrogance, along with slander,
stinginess, quarrels, and disputes;
and amidst those born of dispute, there is slander.
From what cause do dear things arise in the world,
and those cravings that wander through the world?
From what cause do hope and its fulfillment arise?
"Those things which become dear to a person for the sake of the future life—whence is their cause in this world?

He asks: whence is the cause of what is dear? Whence is it born? Whence is it produced? Whence is it generated? Whence does it arise? Whence does it come into being? Whence is it manifested? What is its cause? What is its origin? What is its birth? What is its source? Thus he asks about the root of what is dear... [and so on].
"He asks about its origin, he questions it, he requests it, he entreats it, he seeks to clarify it:
'From what cause, then, do those who are dear in this world arise?
And from what cause do those who are greedy wander in the world?'"
"And those who" refers to khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, householders, renunciants, devas, and humans. "Greed" means that which is greed, the state of being greedy, the state of being greedy;
lust, the act of lusting, the state of being lustful; covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.
"Wander about" means they wander, dwell, move about, conduct themselves, maintain themselves, sustain themselves, and live out their lives.
"In the world"— that is, in the world of the states of misery, the world of humans, the world of devas, the world of aggregates, the world of elements, and the world of sense-bases—
as well as whatever greed wanders in the world:
from what source do both hope and its fulfillment arise?

“From what source do hope and attainment arise? From what are they born? From what are they produced? From what are they generated? From what are they manifested? What is their source, what is their origin, what is their birth, what is their provenance? Thus he asks about the root of hope and attainment...
[as above] ...he asks, he questions, he requests, he entreats, he inspires confidence:
“From what source do hope and attainment arise? [End of Section]
"Those which are for a person's future life":
those which are a person's resorts, islands, refuges, shelters, and havens; those which are the ultimate resort—these are "those which are for a person's future life."
Therefore that created being said:
“From what source, indeed, do dear things arise in this world,
and those cravings which wander about in the world?”
“From what source do hope and its fulfillment arise,
which belong to a person for the sake of the future world?
“Dear things in the world have their source in desire.”
And whatever cravings wander in the world,
both hope and fulfillment,
which arise from this source for a person in the life to come.
One seeks what is dear on account of desire.

"Desire" refers to that which is sensual desire for sense-pleasures, sensual lust, sensual delight, sensual craving, sensual affection, sensual fever, sensual infatuation, sensual clinging, the flood of sensuality, the yoke of sensuality, the clinging to sensuality, and the hindrance of sensual desire.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of desire:
The desire for seeking, the desire for acquisition, the desire for enjoyment, the desire for hoarding, and the desire for relinquishment.
What is the desire for seeking? Here, someone who is already attached, desirous, and filled with longing seeks after forms.
In sounds … in odors … in tastes …
He seeks after tangible objects—
this is the desire for seeking.
What is the desire for acquisition?
In this case, someone who is attached, desirous, and full of longing obtains forms; [he obtains] sounds… smells… [tastes…] tactile objects.
One obtains tastes... tangible objects—
this is the desire for acquisition.
What is the desire for enjoyment?
Here, someone who is attached, desirous, and full of longing enjoys forms, sounds... [and so forth].
He enjoys odors... tastes... tangibles.
This is the desire for enjoyment.
What is the desire for accumulation?
Here, someone who is attached, desirous, and filled with longing makes an accumulation of wealth, thinking, "It will be useful in times of misfortune."
This is the desire for accumulation.
What is the desire for dispersal?

Here, a certain person, being attached, desiring, and having conceived a longing, disperses his wealth among elephant-riders, horse-riders, charioteers, archers, and foot-soldiers, thinking: "These will protect me, guard me, and attend upon me. This is the desire for dispersal.
This is the desire for response.
Regarding "dear things," there are two kinds of dear things:
either sentient beings or conditioned phenomena... [and so forth].
"These beings are dear...
these formations are dear.
One regards as dear those things that have desire as their source."
"Dear things have desire as their source, desire as their origin, are born of desire, and arise from desire— thus,
dear things in the world have desire as their source.
And those who wander through the world with greed..."
"And those who" refers to khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, householders, renunciants, devas, and humans. "Greed" means that which is greed, the state of being greedy, the state of greediness;
it is lust, the state of being lustful, the state of lustfulness; covetousness, greed, the unwholesome root.
"Wander about" means they wander, dwell, move, proceed, maintain themselves, endure, and live on.
"In the world"— in the world of the lower realms …pe… in the world of the sense-bases—
it is those cravings that wander about in the world.
"Hope and fulfillment have their source from this."
"Hope" is said to be craving.
It is lust, infatuation... [as far as] covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.
"Attainment" means that here someone, seeking form, acquires form and finds fulfillment in form.
In sounds … in odors … in tastes …
... tactile objects ...
a family ...
a group ...
… dwelling … gain … fame …
Praise … happiness … robes …
almsfood … lodgings … medicinal requisites for the sick …
the Suttanta … the Vinaya … the Abhidhamma …
The forest-dweller’s practice … the alms-food-eater’s practice … the rag-robe-wearer’s practice …
The practice of possessing only three robes...
the practice of wandering for alms from house to house...
the practice of eating only one meal a day after noon...
The practice of always sitting,
the practice of accepting whatever seat is offered,
and the first jhāna.
the second jhāna … the third jhāna … the fourth jhāna …
the attainment of the base of infinite space … the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness … the attainment of the base of nothingness …

Seeking the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one attains the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and reaches the culmination of that attainment.
"One plows the field with hope;
one sows the seed with hope."
Traders go out to sea with hope as their means of carrying wealth;
with such hope do I stand.
“May this hope of mine be fulfilled.
The fulfillment of hope is called its completion.
Both hope and completion have their source in this.
Hope and attainment have their source here, their origin here, their birth here, and their arising here from desire;
thus hope and attainment have this as their source.
"Those which exist for a person regarding the future"—[this refers to them].
Those who are a person’s ultimate resort, who are an island, a shelter, a refuge, a protection, a final goal, and an ultimate resort—
those who exist for a person’s sake in the world beyond.
Thus the Blessed One said.
“Loving things in this world arise from desire,
as do those cravings that wander through the world;
both hope and its fulfillment have their origin in this.”
“Those which become for a man in the life to come.
From what source, then, does desire arise in the world?
And from what are decisions brought forth?
Anger, false speech, and doubt,
as well as those qualities spoken of by the ascetic—
wherein does desire in the world originate?

"From what cause does desire arise? From what is it born? From what is it produced? From what is it generated? From what is it brought forth? From what does it become manifest? What is its cause, what is its origin, what is its nature, and from what does it come into being? Thus he asks about the root of desire...
[as above] ...he asks, he asks repeatedly, he requests, he entreats, he seeks to clarify:
"From what cause does desire arise in the world?"
"And from what are the determinations (vinicchayā) brought forth?

From what are the determinations brought forth? From what are they born, from what are they produced, from what are they generated, from what are they manifested, from what do they become apparent? What is their source, what is their origin, what is their birth, what is their provenance? Thus he asks about the root of determinations...
[and so on] ...he asks about their origin, he asks again, he entreats, he requests, he beseeches, he propitiates.
And from what have the legal disputes arisen?
Anger, false speech, and doubt.
"Anger" (kodha) refers to such a state as a mental irritation, resentment, hostility, opposition, provocation, incitement, and intense provocation.
Ill will, malice, resentment; the corruption of the mind, mental corruption; anger, being angry, the state of being angry;
hatred, hating, the state of hating; hostility, being hostile, the state of being hostile; opposition, counter-opposition;
ferocity, abruptness, and displeasure of mind.
"False speech" (mosavajja) is said to be lying.
"Doubt" (kathaṅkathā) is said to be perplexity (vicikicchā).
Thus: anger, false speech, and doubt.
"And those states which have been spoken of by the ascetic.

"And those which" means those states that are accompanied by, co-nascent with, conjoined with, and associated with anger, false speech, and doubt; which arise together, cease together, have the same basis, and have the same object—these are called "those states which have been spoken of."
Alternatively, those defilements which are of another kind and of another nature—

these are called "those states. They were spoken by the ascetic— that is, by the one who has stilled evil, the brahmin who has banished evil qualities, the bhikkhu who has shattered the root of the defilements.
"Those teachings spoken by the ascetic, which have been uttered, proclaimed, declared, taught,
laid down, established, revealed, analyzed, made plain, and disclosed,
being free from all bonds of unwholesome roots."
Therefore that created being said:
“Whence, indeed, does desire in the world arise?
And from what are determinations brought forth?”
Anger, false speech, and doubt,
and whatever other things have been spoken of by the recluse—
regarding what is called "pleasant" and "unpleasant" in the world.
Depending upon that, desire arises;
having seen both dissolution and existence in forms,
a person in the world forms a judgment.
Regarding the phrase "What the world calls pleasant and unpleasant":
"Pleasant" refers to pleasant feeling and agreeable objects;
"unpleasant" refers to painful feeling and disagreeable objects.
That which they call "the world"— that which they have said, that which they speak, that which they utter, that which they illuminate, that which they designate— namely,
what they call in the world "the pleasant" and "the unpleasant"—
it is by depending upon that [world] that desire arises.
Depending on the pleasant and the unpleasant, depending on pleasure and pain, depending on joy and grief,
depending on the desirable and the undesirable, depending on attraction and aversion, zeal arises, comes into being, is born, is produced, is generated, and is fully manifested—
thus, "depending on that, zeal arises."
"Having seen the arising and passing away in forms. Regarding "in forms":
this refers to the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements.
What is the arising of forms?
Whatever is the becoming, birth, genesis, production, and manifestation of forms—
this is the becoming of forms.
What is the dissolution of forms?
The exhaustion, passing away, breaking up, dissolution, impermanence, and disappearance of forms—this is the non-existence of forms.

Having seen both non-existence and existence in forms—that is, having seen, perceived, weighed, judged, and discerned both existence and non-existence in forms, and having made it manifest—means: [having done so].
Having seen both dissolution and arising among forms, a person makes a judgment, thinking, "This is the world.
There are two kinds of judgments: [the judgment of the world and the judgment of the Dhamma].
The determination regarding craving and the determination regarding views.
How does one make the determination regarding craving?
Here, for a certain person, wealth that has not yet arisen does not arise, and wealth that has already arisen goes to destruction.
It occurs to him:
"By what means is it that wealth not yet arisen does not arise for me, and wealth already arisen goes to destruction?

Then it occurs to him: "For me, who is devoted to the practice of indulgence in liquor, wine, and intoxicants—which are the basis for negligence—it is that wealth not yet arisen does not arise, and wealth already arisen goes to destruction."
For me, who was devoted to the practice of wandering for alms at improper times, wealth that had not yet arisen did not arise, and wealth that had already arisen went to ruin; for me,
who was devoted to frequenting social gatherings… for me,
who was devoted to the practice of intoxicants and negligence… [wealth that had not yet arisen did not arise, and wealth that had already arisen went to ruin].
"Having formed the knowledge: 'For me, who is devoted to the practice of associating with evil friends, wealth that has not yet arisen does not arise, and wealth that has already arisen goes to ruin;

for me, who is devoted to the practice of laziness, wealth that has not yet arisen does not arise, and wealth that has already arisen goes to ruin,' one does not resort to the six doors of loss regarding wealth."
He pursues the sources of income for enjoyments.
In this way too, he makes a determination regarding craving.
Alternatively, he engages in agriculture, trade, cattle-rearing, archery, government service, or some other craft.
In this way, he makes a determination regarding craving.
How does he make a determination regarding views?
When the eye has arisen, he knows: [it is impermanent].
Thinking, "My self has arisen," when the eye has disappeared, he knows:
"My self has disappeared; my self is gone.
In this way, too, he makes a determination based on views.
In the ear … in the nose … in the tongue …
In the body … in form … in sound …
When [a feeling] has arisen in regard to an odor... a taste... or a tangible object, he knows it.
Thinking, “My self has arisen,” when the tangible object has disappeared, he knows:
“My self has disappeared; my self has vanished.
In this way, he forms, generates, produces, brings about, and fully manifests a determination of views.
A "creature" (jantu) is a being, a person, a human, ... [and so on] ... a mortal.
A "world" (loka) refers to the world of the lower realms ... [and so on] ... or the world of the sense bases—it is regarding these that a creature makes a determination in the world.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“That which the world calls ‘pleasant’ and ‘unpleasant,’ depending upon that, desire arises.”
"Having seen both dissolution and origination in forms,
a person in the world forms a judgment.
Anger, false speech, and doubt—
Even these phenomena exist as only a pair;
one who is free from doubt should train in the path of knowledge,
for these phenomena were taught by the Recluse after he had realized them.
Anger, false speech, and doubt.
"Anger" refers to such a state of mental resentment or repulsion... [as previously described] ...
"False speech" is said to be lying.
“Doubt” (kathaṅkathā) is said to be perplexity (vicikicchā).
Anger arises based on a desirable object; anger also arises based on an undesirable object.
False speech arises based on a desirable object; false speech also arises based on an undesirable object.
Doubt arises based on a desirable object; doubt also arises based on an undesirable object.
How does anger arise based on an undesirable object?
Anger arises based on an object that is undesirable by its very nature.
"Anger arises [thinking], 'He has done me harm';
anger arises [thinking], 'He is doing me harm';
anger arises [thinking], 'He will do me harm.'"
Anger arises [thinking]: "He has acted for the harm of one who is dear and pleasing to me," or "He is acting for their harm," or "He will act for their harm."
Anger arises [in one] thinking: "He acted for the welfare of one who is unpleasant and disagreeable to me," or "He is acting for their welfare," or "He will act for their welfare."
Thus, anger arises dependent upon an undesirable object.
How does anger arise dependent upon a desirable object?
Anger also arises in one who fears the loss of a desirable object.
Anger arises even when something is being snatched away;
anger arises even when it has already been snatched away.
Anger also arises in one who fears the alteration of a cherished object.
Anger arises when something is changing,
and anger also arises when it has already changed.
Thus, anger arises dependent upon a desirable object.
How does false speech arise based on an undesirable object?
Here, someone is bound by a tether;
for the sake of being released from that bond, he speaks a deliberate lie...
Or bound with a rope-bond...
or bound with an iron-shackle bond...
or bound with a cane-bond...
Or bound by a creeper-fetter...
or bound by a throwing-fetter... or bound by an enclosure-fetter...
Whether he is bound by the confinement of a village, a town, a city, or a kingdom, or bound by the confinement of a district,
he speaks a deliberate lie for the sake of release from that confinement.
Thus, false speech arises dependent upon an undesirable object.
How does false speech arise dependent upon a desirable object?
Here, someone speaks a deliberate lie for the sake of pleasing forms...
of pleasant sounds … of odors … of tastes …
For the sake of tactile objects … for the sake of robes … for the sake of almsfood …
One speaks a deliberate lie for the sake of lodgings, or for the sake of medicinal requisites as support for the sick.
Thus, false speech arises based on a desirable object.
How does doubt arise based on an undesirable object?
"Shall I be freed from eye disease, or shall I not be freed from eye disease?
Shall I be freed from ear disease... [and so forth].
From diseases of the nose … from diseases of the tongue … from diseases of the body …
From diseases of the head … from diseases of the ear … from diseases of the mouth …
“Will I indeed be freed from this dental disease, or will I not be freed from this dental disease?
In this way, doubt arises based on an undesirable object.
How does doubt arise based on a desirable object?
“Shall I obtain pleasing forms, or shall I not obtain pleasing forms?
Shall I obtain pleasing sounds… pleasing odors…?”
In tastes … in tangibles … in clans …
The group … the residence … the gain …
fame … praise … happiness …
robes … almsfood … lodgings …
“Requisites for medicinal treatment as support for the sick.
Thus, based on such a desirable object, doubt arises:
anger, falsehood, and doubt.

"These phenomena also exist as a mere duality": when pleasure and pain exist, when happiness and suffering exist, when joy and grief exist, when the desirable and the undesirable exist, and when attraction and repulsion exist— being present, found, and obtainable—
these phenomena also exist as a mere duality.
"One who is full of doubt trains for the path of knowledge.
Knowledge itself is the path of knowledge; the object of knowledge is the path of knowledge; and the states co-existent with knowledge are also the path of knowledge.
Just as the noble path is the noble path, the path of the gods is the path of the gods, and the path of Brahmā is the path of Brahmā.
In the same way, knowledge itself is the path of knowledge; the object of knowledge is also the path of knowledge; and the states that coexist with knowledge are also the path of knowledge.
Training means the three trainings:
the training in higher virtue, the training in higher consciousness, and the training in higher wisdom.
What is the training in higher virtue?

Here, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.
This is the minor aggregate of virtue...
The great aggregate of virtue...
virtue is the foundation, the beginning, the conduct, the restraint, the control, the entrance, the foremost gateway for the attainment of wholesome states—
this is the training in higher virtue.
What is the training in the higher mind?
Here, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures … [as above] … enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
This is the training in higher mind.
What is the training in higher wisdom?
Here, a bhikkhu is wise; he possesses the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering.
Thus one understands as it really is: "This is suffering" ... [and so on] ... one understands as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering";

one understands as it really is: "These are the taints" ... [and so on] ... one understands as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints"—this is the training in higher wisdom.
"One who is full of doubt trains for the path of knowledge.
A person who is full of doubt— one who is skeptical, scrupulous, wavering, and possessed of uncertainty—
might train in higher virtue, train in higher mind, and train in higher wisdom for the sake of attaining knowledge, for the touch of knowledge, and for the realization of knowledge.
One should train by reflecting upon these three trainings;
one should train with knowledge;
one should train with vision.
One should train while reflecting;
one should train while resolving the mind;
one should train while being resolved through faith.
Exerting energy, one should train;
establishing mindfulness, one should train;
concentrating the mind, one should train.
One should train while understanding with wisdom;
one should train while directly knowing what is to be directly known;
one should train while fully understanding what is to be fully understood.
One should train in abandoning what is to be abandoned;
one should train in developing what is to be developed;
one should train in realizing what is to be realized—one should practice it, practice it thoroughly, and conduct oneself by undertaking it.
"One who is full of doubt should train in the path of knowledge.

'The Dhamma has been proclaimed by the ascetic after he had known it'—having known means having known, understood, weighed, scrutinized, clarified, and made manifest; it has been proclaimed, uttered, declared, taught, laid down, established, revealed, analyzed, made plain, and disclosed."

“Having known, understood, weighed, scrutinized, and fully clarified that ‘All conditioned phenomena are impermanent,’ it has been stated, proclaimed, declared, taught, established, set forth, revealed, analyzed, made plain, and disclosed:
‘All conditioned phenomena are suffering’ … ‘All phenomena are non-self’ …”
“With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise”… “with birth as condition,
aging-and-death arises”… “from the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease”… [and so on]… “from the cessation of birth, aging-and-death ceases.”
“With the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of aging and death”… “This is suffering”… [and so on] … “This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.”
“‘These are the taints’ … ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of the taints’ … ‘These phenomena are to be directly known’ …”
“These phenomena are to be fully understood,” … “these phenomena are to be abandoned,” … “these phenomena are to be developed,” …
“These phenomena are to be realized”:
[the arising, passing away, gratification, danger, and escape] of the six bases of contact;
… of the five aggregates of clinging; … [and so forth].
Having known, understood, weighed, scrutinized, and fully clarified that "whatever is subject to arising is all subject to cessation" regarding the four great elements...
these [teachings] have been spoken, proclaimed, declared, taught, made known, established, set forth, and revealed.
It has been analyzed, laid bare, and made manifest.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“It is with direct knowledge, monks, that I teach the Dhamma, not without direct knowledge.”
“Bhikkhus, I teach the Dhamma with its basis, not without its basis;
I teach the Dhamma with its wonders, not without its wonders.
For me, bhikkhus, when teaching the Dhamma through direct knowledge, not without direct knowledge, I teach the Dhamma with its basis...”
He teaches the Dhamma with a foundation, not without a foundation; he teaches the Dhamma that is wondrous, not one that is not wondrous.
Therefore, advice should be given and instruction should be provided.

And it is enough, monks, for your satisfaction, enough for your gladness, enough for your joy, that the Blessed One is a perfectly enlightened Buddha, the Dhamma is well-expounded, and the Saṅgha is practicing rightly... [as before]...
And while this exposition was being spoken, the ten-thousandfold world system trembled.
Having known this, the ascetic proclaimed these teachings.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Anger, false speech, and doubt—
even these phenomena, though they appear as pairs, exist only as such.
One who harbors doubt should train in the path of knowledge.”
“Having known the teachings proclaimed by the ascetic, [he asked:
‘From what source do the pleasant and the unpleasant arise?
In the absence of what do these two not come to be?’”
"Tell me this matter: from what source do both non-existence and existence arise?
And from what source do the pleasant and the unpleasant arise?"

“From what source do the pleasant and the unpleasant arise? From what are they born? From what are they produced? From what are they generated? From what are they brought forth? From what have they become manifest? What is their source, what is their origin, what is their birth, what is their provenance?
Thus he asks about the root of the pleasant and the unpleasant; … [as before] … he asks, he questions, he requests, he entreats, he makes clear:
“From what source do the pleasant and the unpleasant arise?”
"When this is absent, these do not come to be": when what is absent,
unperceived, non-existent, and unapprehended, do pleasure and pain not come to be, do they not arise, do they not originate, do they not come into being, do they not manifest,
do they not fully manifest?— when this is absent, these do not come to be.
"Both non-existence and existence—this is the meaning.
What is the existence of the pleasant and the unpleasant?
That which is the existence, the source, the birth, the arising, the production, the manifestation, and the appearance of the pleasant and the unpleasant.
This is the occurrence of the pleasant and the unpleasant.
What is the dissolution of the pleasant and the unpleasant?
It is the destruction, passing away, breaking up, disintegration, impermanence, and disappearance of the pleasant and the unpleasant.
This is the dissolution of the pleasant and the unpleasant.
That which is called "this meaning" or "the ultimate meaning"—it is both dissolution and existence; this is what is meant by "this meaning."
"Tell me this, from what source it arises":
*Etam* refers to that which I ask, that which I entreat, that which I beseech, that which I inspire with confidence.
*Pabrūhi*: speak, say, declare, teach, point out, establish, set forth, open up, analyze, make plain, reveal.
Tell me this:
"From what source" means from whatever source, from whatever origin, from whatever birth, from whatever arising—
that tell me, "from what source."
Therefore that created being said:
“From what source do the pleasant and the unpleasant arise?
When what is absent do these two not come to be?”
"Tell me this matter, from what source it arises: both non-existence and existence.
Pleasure and pain have contact as their source."
When contact does not exist, these do not come to be;
both non-becoming and becoming—
this matter I declare to you has its source in this.
"Pleasant and unpleasant [feeling] have contact as their source.
Dependent upon a contact to be experienced as pleasant, a pleasant feeling arises.

With the cessation of that very same contact to be experienced as pleasant, the corresponding sensation—the pleasant feeling that arose dependent upon that contact to be experienced as pleasant—ceases and subsides.
In dependence on a contact to be experienced as painful, a painful feeling arises.
With the cessation of that very same contact to be experienced as painful, that feeling to be experienced as painful—which had arisen in dependence on that contact—ceases and subsides.
In dependence on a contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises.

With the cessation of that very contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, the corresponding feeling to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant—which had arisen in dependence upon that contact—ceases and subsides.
"Pleasant and unpleasant have contact as their source.
Thus, pleasant and unpleasant have contact as their source, contact as their origin, contact as their birth, and contact as their arising.
"Pleasant and unpleasant [feeling] have contact as their source.
When contact is absent, they do not come to be;

they have no cause. When contact is absent, being unobservable and non-apprehendable, pleasant and unpleasant [feelings] do not exist, do not arise, are not born, are not produced, are not generated, are not manifested, do not appear, and do not become manifest.
"When contact is absent, these do not come to be;
both non-existence (vibhava) and existence (bhava) have this as their meaning.
Both the view of existence and the view of non-existence have contact as their source.
"That which is this meaning" means "that which is the ultimate meaning"— namely, both non-existence and existence.
"I declare this to you as having its source from here."
"Regarding that which you ask, that which you entreat, that which you request, and that by which you show confidence:
'I shall speak,' I say, I declare, I teach, I describe, I establish, I reveal, I analyze, I make plain, I illuminate— this is what I tell you."
"Having this as its source" means: having contact as its source, having contact as its origin, born of contact, arisen from contact—this, I tell you, is "having this as its source.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Pleasant and unpleasant [feelings] have contact as their source;
when contact is absent, these do not come to be.
Both non-existence and existence—this is the meaning.”
"I tell you this: it has its source from this.
But from what source does contact arise in the world, and from what are possessions brought forth?
When what is absent is there no sense of "mine"?
When what has vanished do contacts not touch?
From what source, then, does contact arise in the world?

“From what is contact its source? From what is it born? From what is it produced? From what does it arise? From what is it fully manifested? From what has it become evident? What is its source, what is its origin, what is its nature, what is its provenance?
Thus he asks about the root of contact, asks about its cause … [and so on] … asks about its origin, inquires, requests, entreats, and seeks to clarify:
“From what source in the world does contact arise?”

"And from where have possessions arisen?"—he asks about the root of possessions, he asks about their cause: "From where have possessions arisen? From where were they born? From where did they originate?

From where were they produced? From where were they brought forth? From where did they become manifest? What is their source? What is their origin? What is their birth? What is their provenance? ... [and so on] ...
...he asks about the cause of possessions. ... [and so on] ...
"He asks, he questions repeatedly, he entreats, he implores, he seeks to please:
'Whence have possessions arisen?
When what is absent is there no sense of "mine"?'"
When something is non-existent, unperceived, absent, and not found, there is no sense of "mine"; it does not exist, is not present, is not perceived, and is not found.
It has been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and calmed; it is incapable of arising again, burnt up by the fire of knowledge.
Thus, when something is non-existent, there is no sense of "mine."
"When what has vanished do contacts not touch?
When what has vanished, disappeared, passed beyond, transcended, and gone beyond, contacts do not touch—that is:
"When what has vanished do contacts not touch?"
Therefore that created being said:
“From what cause, then, does contact arise in the world?
And from what are possessions brought forth?”
"When nothing exists, there is no sense of 'mine';
when nothing has ceased, contacts do not touch.
Contact depends upon name-and-form.
Possessions have their origin in desire;
when desire is not present, there is no sense of "mine.
When form has vanished, contacts do not touch.
“Dependent on name-and-form, contact arises.
Eye-consciousness arises dependent on the eye and forms; the meeting of these three is contact.
The eye, the forms, and the mental factors associated with them—excluding the eye-contact itself—are “name” within the form.
In this way, contact arises dependent upon both name and form.
Dependent upon the ear and sounds, ear-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three is contact.
The ear, the sounds, and the associated mental states—excluding ear-contact itself—are included within "name" in relation to form.
In this way, contact arises dependent upon both name-and-form.
Dependent upon the nose and odors, nose-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three is contact.
The nose, the odors, and the mental factors associated with them—excluding the nose-contact itself—are "name" within the form-sphere.
In this way, contact arises dependent upon both name and form.
Dependent upon the tongue and tastes, tongue-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three is contact.
Herein, the tongue and the tastes belong to the form aggregate, while the associated mental states—excluding the tongue-contact itself—belong to the name aggregate.
In this way, contact arises dependent on both name and form.
Dependent on the body and tangible objects, body-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three is contact.
Here, the body and the tangible objects—excluding the body-contact itself—are included within form, while the associated mental states are included within name.
In this way, contact arises dependent on both name and form.
Mental consciousness arises dependent on the mind and mental objects; the meeting of these three is contact.
The physical basis is form within form; the mental factors associated with it—excluding mental contact—are name within form.
Thus, contact also arises dependent upon name-and-form.
"Possessions have desire as their source":
here, "desire" refers to craving.
Whatever lust, infatuation, ... [as above] ... covetousness, greed, which is a root of unwholesomeness.
"Possessions" means two kinds of possessions:
the possession of craving and the possession of views, ... [as above] ...
This is the appropriation of craving... [and so on] ...this is the appropriation of views.
These appropriations have desire as their source.
Possessions have longing as their source, longing as their cause, longing as their condition, longing as their origin, and longing as their provenance— thus, possessions have longing as their source.
Without the cessation of longing, there is no sense of "mine."
"Desire" (icchā) is said to be craving (taṇhā).
That which is lust, infatuation … [as above] … covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.
"Possessiveness" (mamatta) refers to two kinds of possessiveness:
The intoxication of craving and the intoxication of views … [as above] … this is the intoxication of craving … [as above] … this is the intoxication of views.
"Because desire does not exist, there is no sense of 'mine'":
when desire does not exist—that is, when it is not found, is unapprehendable, absent, non-existent, not present, not manifest, and unapprehendable;

when it has been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and tranquillized; when it is incapable of arising again and has been consumed by the fire of knowledge—it is said that because desire does not exist, there is no sense of "mine."
Through the relinquishing of desire, there is no sense of "mine.
When form has vanished, contacts do not touch.
"Form" refers to the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements.
"Form has been abolished": form is abolished in four ways—by abolition through knowledge, by abolition through investigation, by abolition through abandoning, and by abolition through surmounting.
How is form abolished by abolition through knowledge?
One knows form:
one knows and sees, "Whatever form there is, all that form consists of the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements.
In this way, through the manifestation of what is known, form becomes manifest.
How does form become manifest through the manifestation of investigation?
Having known it thus, one investigates form as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor, as a dart, as a calamity,
as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as a plague, as a disaster, as a terror, as a menace, as fickle, as perishable, as unstable, as offering no shelter.
As being without protection, without refuge, empty, vain, void, non-self, fraught with danger, subject to change,
pithless, the root of evil, a murderer, a source of destruction, accompanied by taints, conditioned, the bait of Māra, subject to birth, subject to aging,
subject to sickness, subject to death, and subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
He scrutinizes it by way of its being subject to defilement, its origination, its passing away, its gratification, its danger, and the escape from it.
In this way, form becomes manifest through the manifestation of scrutiny.
How does form become manifest through the manifestation of abandoning?
Having investigated in this way, one abandons desire and lust for form, dispels it, brings it to an end, and causes it to cease.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, whatever desire and lust there is for form, abandon that."
"In this way, that form will be abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future.
In this way, form becomes manifest through manifestation by means of abandoning.
How does form become manifest through manifestation by means of transcending?
For one who has attained the four formless attainments, forms have become non-existent, have been made non-existent, have been transcended, have been fully transcended, and have been passed beyond.
Thus, by means of transcendence, form becomes non-existent.
By these four reasons, form becomes non-existent.
"When form has vanished, contacts do not touch.
When form has vanished, been made to vanish, transcended, fully transcended, and passed beyond, the five contacts do not touch:
eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, and body-contact.
When form has vanished, contacts do not touch.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Contact depends upon name-and-form."
Possessions have desire as their source;
when desire is not present, there is no sense of "mine.
When form has vanished, contacts do not touch one.
How does form disappear for one who has attained [this state]?
And how do pleasure and pain also disappear?
Tell me this, how they disappear.
"The thought occurred to me:
'May I know that—how does form cease for one who has come together?
" 'For one who has come together' means: how for one who has come together, how for one who has practiced, how for one who is conducting himself?
For one who is acting, maintaining, sustaining, and supporting [the body], how does form vanish, dissolve, pass away, transcend, and go beyond? Thus:
"How does form vanish for one who is composed? means this.

"How is it that pleasure and pain are overcome? means: how are pleasure and pain overcome, how are they dispelled, how are they transcended, how are they fully transcended, how are they passed beyond?
Thus: "How is it that pleasure and pain are overcome? Tell me this, how they are overcome."
"That which I ask, that which I entreat, that which I beseech, that which I propitiate"—this is "the *etaṃ*.
"'Tell it to me' means: tell it to me, declare it, teach it, lay it out, establish it, open it up, analyze it, make it plain, and reveal it"—this is "the *me pabrūhi*."
Tell me this:
how does it cease? Tell me how it ceases—that is, how it is made to disappear, transcended, fully surmounted, and passed beyond.
Tell me how it ceases.
"May we know that"—such was my thought.
"May we know that": may we know it, may we understand it, may we discern it, may we penetrate it, may we pierce through it—thus, "may we know that."
"Thus was my mind," "thus was my mind," "thus was my consciousness," "thus was my intention," "thus was my cognition"—let us know that "thus was my mind.
Therefore, that created being said: [this is what he meant].
“How does form vanish for one who has attained [this state]?
And how do pleasure and pain also vanish?
Tell me this, how it vanishes.”
"May I know that"— such was my thought.
Neither perceiving nor non-perceiving,
neither non-perceiving nor one whose perception has vanished;
For one who has thus composed himself, form disappears;
for conceptual proliferation is rooted in perception.
He is neither one who perceives, nor one who does not perceive.
Those who abide in ordinary perception are called "possessors of perception"; he does not abide in ordinary perception.
Those who are insane or whose minds are deranged are called "possessors of distorted perception"; he is neither insane nor is his mind deranged.
Thus, he is neither a possessor of perception nor a possessor of distorted perception.
"Neither unconscious nor one whose perception has vanished":
those who have attained cessation and the non-percipient beings are called "unconscious," but he has neither attained cessation nor is he a non-percipient being.
Those who have obtained the four formless attainments are called "one whose perception has vanished," but he has not obtained the four formless attainments.
Nor is he percipient of the non-existent, nor is he one whose perception has vanished.
For one who is thus composed, "form vanishes.
Here, a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure ... [as before] ... enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
Thus, when the mind is concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from defilements, become pliant, wieldy, steady,
and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines the mind toward the attainment of the base of infinite space;
this is called "one who possesses the path of the formless."
For one who is thus composed, thus practicing, thus conducting oneself, thus behaving, thus maintaining, thus preserving,
and thus sustaining [the practice], form dissolves, is dissolved, is transcended, is fully transcended, and is surpassed. Thus,
for one who is thus composed, form dissolves.
"For proliferation-conceptualization has perception as its source.

Proliferation-conceptualization is indeed proliferation itself: the proliferation-conceptualization of craving, the proliferation-conceptualization of views, and the proliferation-conceptualization of conceit. It has perception as its source, perception as its origin, perception as its birth, and perception as its provenance—thus, "proliferation-conceptualization has perception as its source."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Neither perceiving perceptions, nor perceiving non-perceptions,
nor non-perceiving, nor having perceptions extinguished;”
"For one who has thus attained, form ceases;
for conceptual proliferation (papañca-saṅkhā) has its source in perception.
Thus, what we asked, you have explained to us.
We ask you another thing, please tell us that:
To what extent do some wise ones here say that purity for a *yakkha* has been attained?
Or do they say something else besides this?
That which we asked, has he not explained it?
That which we asked, entreated, requested, and inspired with confidence.

"Has he not proclaimed? Has it not been declared, fully declared, explained, taught, laid down, established, revealed, analyzed, made plain, and manifested?"—that which we asked, has he not proclaimed it?
"We ask another thing; please speak on that."
"We ask you about another thing, we entreat you about another thing, we beseech you about another thing, we inspire confidence in you regarding another thing; we ask you further.
Please explain that!"—in "Please explain," it means: explain, declare, teach, set forth, establish, reveal, analyze, make plain, and manifest.
Thus, "we ask you about another thing; please explain that."
"‘This much, indeed, is the pinnacle,’ so some wise ones here say regarding the purification of a *yakkha*.

Some ascetics and brahmins declare, speak, utter, illuminate, and express that these formless attainments (*arūpasamāpatti*) are the pinnacle, the best, the most distinguished, the foremost, the supreme, and the most excellent.
‘Of a *yakkha*’ means of a being, a man, a youth, a person, an individual, a soul, a creature, a person, a human being."
"Purity" means purity, purification, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, and total emancipation.

"Here, these wise ones" refers to those here who speak as wise men, who speak with steadfastness, who speak according to the method, who speak according to reason, who speak according to characteristics, who speak according to cause, who speak according to ground, and who speak according to their own tenets—it is to this extent, indeed, that some here say there is purity for a *yakkha*. These are the wise ones here.
Or do they say there is something else beyond this?
Or do some ascetics and brahmins, having transcended, surpassed, and passed beyond these formless attainments,
claim that there is another purification, cleansing, complete purity, and liberation for a *yakkha* superior to these formless attainments?
"Do they speak, talk, say, illuminate, and express liberation and complete liberation—
or do they speak of something else besides this?
Thus spoke that emanated being.
“What we asked you, you have explained to us;
now we ask another thing—please tell us that.
Do some say that this is the ultimate extent?”
“Do the wise here declare the purification of a *yakkha*,
or do they say there is something else besides this?
Thus some speak even to this extent.
The wise here declare the purification of a yakkha; yet some,
skilled in the declarations of the virtuous, speak of a time when there is no residue remaining.
"Some wise ones here say that purity for a *yakkha* reaches even this far.

There being some recluses and brahmins who are eternalists, they say, speak, declare, proclaim, illuminate, and express that these formless attainments are the highest, the best, the most excellent, the foremost, the supreme, and the preeminent.
‘For a *yakkha’ means for a being, a human, a youth, a person, an individual, a soul, a creature, a progenitor, a descendant of Indra, or a mortal."
"Purity" means purity, complete purity, total purity; liberation, complete liberation, total liberation.

"Here, some wise ones" means here those who speak as wise men, who speak with steadfastness, who speak according to logic, who speak according to reason, who speak according to characteristics, who speak according to cause, who speak according to ground, and who speak according to their own tenets—some of them say that even this much is the purity of a *yakkha* here for those who are wise.
But at one time some among them say: "In the state where there is no substrate remaining, there is the excellence of the wholesome.
Among those very same recluses and brahmins, some recluses and brahmins who are annihilationists, being terrified of existence, delight in non-existence;
they speak of the evenness, the peace, the complete stilling, the cessation, and the subsiding of the being, saying: "What then, sir, is this self [in relation] to the body?"
"Differences are cut off, destroyed, and do not exist after death; to this extent it is 'without residue' (anupādisesa).

Regarding "proclamations of the wholesome" (kusalāvadāna): these are proclamations of the wholesome, proclamations of the wise, proclamations of the steadfast, proclamations of the methodical, proclamations of the causal, proclamations of the characteristic, proclamations of the rational, proclamations of the foundational, and proclamations according to one's own tenets—it is regarding these that some at one time speak of "proclamations of the wholesome" in relation to the state without residue.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Some wise ones here say that even this much is the purification of a yakkha.”
"But some among them at times speak,
being skilled in discourse regarding the state where nothing remains.
Having understood that these [beings] are dependent [on conditions],...
Having understood the supports, the sage investigates them;
having understood and being liberated, he does not enter into dispute.
The wise one does not strive for existence after existence.
"And having known these as dependent": "these" refers to those who hold views. "Dependent" means:

having known them as dependent on the eternalist view, having known them as dependent on the annihilationist view, and having known them as dependent on both the eternalist and annihilationist views—having thus understood, weighed, scrutinized, and clarified them, making them manifest.
And having known these as dependent, the sage, having known the supports, is one who reflects. "The sage" (munī): [the following is the commentary].
"Silence" is said to be knowledge... [as above] ...having transcended the net of attachments, he is a sage (*muni*).

Having known that they rely on the view of eternalism, having known that they rely on the view of annihilationism, and having known that they rely on both the views of eternalism and annihilationism—having understood, weighed, scrutinized, and fully analyzed them—he is "one who investigates.
Knowing that "he is wise, possessed of wisdom, intelligent, knowledgeable, discerning, and sagacious," the sage, as one who investigates, relies upon these [conditions].
"Knowing, one is liberated; one does not enter into dispute": having known, understood, weighed, scrutinized, and fully clarified [the truth].
"Liberated" means freed, liberated, completely liberated, thoroughly liberated by means of the ultimate liberation through non-clinging.

Having known, understood, weighed, scrutinized, and fully clarified that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent," one is freed, liberated, completely liberated, and thoroughly liberated by means of the ultimate liberation through non-clinging.
“‘All conditioned phenomena are suffering’ … ‘All phenomena are non-self’ … ‘Whatever is subject to arising is all subject to cessation’”—

having known this, having understood it, having weighed it, having scrutinized it, having clarified it, and having made it manifest, one is liberated, fully liberated, completely liberated, and thoroughly liberated by means of the ultimate liberation through non-clinging.
"Knowing this, he is liberated.
"He does not engage in dispute" means he does not quarrel, he does not argue, he does not contend, he does not dispute, and he does not cause strife.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Aggivessana, a bhikkhu whose mind is thus liberated does not agree with anyone, nor does he dispute with anyone; he employs the speech used in the world without clinging to it.
Having known this, one who is liberated does not enter into dispute.
The wise man does not strive for existence after existence.
"From existence to existence" means: for existence—that is, for kamma-existence, for renewed existence, for sense-sphere existence;
for kamma-existence, for sense-sphere existence, for renewed existence, for fine-material existence; for kamma-existence, for fine-material existence, for renewed existence, for immaterial existence;

for kamma-existence, for immaterial existence, for renewed existence, for repeated renewed existence, for repeated rebirths, for repeated destinations, for repeated births, for repeated rebirth-linkings.
He does not agree with, does not encounter, does not grasp, does not misapprehend, and does not adhere to repeated personal existence or repeated rebirth.
"The wise one" means he is wise, learned, possessed of wisdom, intelligent, knowledgeable, discerning, and sagacious.
The wise one does not incline toward existence or non-existence.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Having understood that these are dependent...”
Having understood the dependencies, that sage investigates them;
having understood and being liberated, he does not engage in dispute;
the wise one does not strive for existence after existence.
The eleventh exposition: the discourse on quarrels and disputes.
